\subsection{Transimpedance Stage}\label{ss:tiaamp}

The transimpedance stage is amplifier A2 of the potentiostat. It holds the working
electrode (WE) at $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ on its inverting input and converts the electrode
current to a voltage through a feedback resistor $R_f$ from output to WE. Both current
directions pass through $R_f$ by Kirchhoff's current law, which is how bipolar sensing
is met without a current mirror:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:tia-transfer}
  V_{\mathrm{OUT}} = v_{\mathrm{cm}} - I_{\mathrm{WE}} R_f ,
\end{equation}

with $I_{\mathrm{WE}}$ positive into the WE node, so the ADC sees offset binary around
the $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ code. (The test source in \texttt{TiaFbTB} sweeps the opposite
sign, which is why Figure~\ref{fig:tia-dc} has a positive slope.) In the assembled
channel $R_f$ is a 16-tap string, \SIrange{35}{560}{\kilo\ohm}; one instance is used per
channel and all four share the bias generator of Section~\ref{ss:biasgen-local}.

The amplifier is a two-stage Miller-compensated design (Figure~\ref{fig:tia-core}):
PMOS input pair, NMOS current-mirror load, then a common-source NMOS driver with a PMOS
current-source load, compensated by a MIM capacitor in series with a nulling resistor.
Two consequences run through everything below. A PMOS input pair places the common-mode
range against \texttt{vss}, which is what holding an electrode near ground requires, at
the cost of \SI{0.44}{\volt} at the top (Table~\ref{tab:tia-range}). And the second
stage is class~A, so it sinks with a driven device but sources only a fixed bias
current --- \SIrange{13.6}{15.6}{\micro\ampere} against a sinking capability this run
does not resolve (Table~\ref{tab:tia-drive}).

The characterisation is schematic-level, with no extracted parasitics, from four
testbenches whose scope differs in ways that matter:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{UnityFeedbackTB} and \texttt{StepUnityFeedbackTB} close the amplifier in
unity feedback with a \SI{5}{\pico\farad} load: gain, margins, offset, noise, settling.
\item \texttt{DriveTB} adds a swept DC load current to that configuration, giving the
output drive limits.
\item \texttt{SlewOpenLoopTB} drives the amplifier open-loop, giving the slew rates.
\item \texttt{TiaFbTB} is the only bench that closes the transimpedance loop, wrapping
$R_f = \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}$ to WE and loading WE with \SI{1}{\micro\farad} of
double-layer capacitance. \textbf{Every closed-loop figure comes from here, and the
amplifier's own margins do not describe this loop.}
\end{itemize}

Three limits on coverage. Only the \emph{maximum}-gain setting was simulated, with an
ideal resistor rather than the 16-tap string. The run is corners only, so offset,
matching and every yield figure are uncharacterised. And the run's fifth testbench,
\texttt{TypOpenLoopTB}, is not used: its open-loop DC operating point sits at
\SI{0.23}{\volt} with the second stage out of its linear region, so its AC gain is not
the open-loop gain --- Figure~\ref{fig:tia-loopgain} supersedes it.
